newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - TECHNICLONE READIES NEW DRUG.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - TECHNICLONE READIES NEW DRUG.

text.p: Sixteen years after Techniclone Inc was formed to develop a safer, more precise cancer treatment, it is starting to see its efforts pay off.

The Tustin, Calif.-based research company expects its first drug, a lymphoma treatment called LYM-1, to win Food and Drug Administration approval by late 1998 or early 1999, chief financial officer William Moding said in a recent interview.
"We expect that, since this is a life-threatening disease with no other treatments available for its advanced stages, the FDA will act on our application quickly," Moding said.

Techniclone has not yet applied for approval of LYM-1. It first has to conduct a Phase III trial, which it expects to begin shortly. But Moding said Techniclone is confident of approval based on the results of earlier clinical trials that fell "within the guidelines the FDA has given us verbally."
LYM-1 is the first in a series of drugs Techniclone hopes to develop that will change the way cancer is treated.
The drug is a radioactive isotope attached to an antibody, which when injected to the site of a tumor, heads right for the cancer cells and avoids surrounding tissue.
Because it has such a specific delivery mechanism, LYM-1 can be administered in larger quantities than are given in traditional radiation therapy.
"We think this is a prime time for the company," Moding said. "The fundamentals are only getting better."

Although it experienced delays in earlier clinical trials, Techniclone expects the upcoming Phase III trial will run smoothly and be "much easier" he said. Assuming the company stays on schedule, he estimates it could be profitable by the year 2000. But this optimism is not reflected in the company's market valuation. Techniclone's stock now sells $4 a share, well off its high for the year of over $7.

While developing and winning approval of new drugs is usually a long process, few companies have had their patience tested as much as Techniclone. It has had repeated delays, initially because of its limited financial resources and later due to a disagreement with a partner for its lymphoma treatment. About five years ago, it was forced to buy the license back and start over with a new partner.
In the meantime, what was once its unique approach to treating cancer has lost some of its novelty.

Several companies now are conducting research based on more specific delivery mechanisms. Two companies, IDEC Pharmaceuticals Corp and Genentech Inc recently developed another lymphoma drug, Rituxan, which is also delivered directly to the site of the cancer and is expected to win FDA approval by the end of the year.

But Moding said Rituxan is not a treatment for advanced lymphoma, a market that remains untapped. About 240,000 U.S. patients suffer from lymphoma and it is unclear how many of them have a late stage form of the disease.

Techniclone is also working on more advanced technologies that would take a drug to the core of a solid tumor, so it can attack it from the inside out. In tests on eight Chinese patients with brain cancer, this tumor necrosis therapy produced remission of at least a year in seven patients.
Such treatments eventually could offer new hope of treating the most difficult to treat cancers, such as lung cancer, where surgery to remove the cancer is often not an option.
"It opens up areas of cancer where there are no treatments, or where they are not very effective," Moding said.
